value: API and EIA crude-inventory surprises both move 15-minute CL returns; EIA effect about twice API's
detail: Ye and Karali (2015), AAEA poster (precursor of Energy Economics 2016). 15-minute windows 10:25-10:40 ET (EIA) and 16:25-16:40 ET (API). Coefficients on crude shock: API -0.134/-0.126, EIA -0.231/-0.247. Absorption beyond 15 minutes not tested. 11 of 50 EIA reports produced significant return jumps; only 1 jump in the API window.
quote: The impact of crude oil inventory surprises in EIA report is almost twice the impact of the surprise in API reports. | In total, 11 out of 50 EIA reports generated significant return jumps.

value: jump clustering at the former pit open (8:55-9:10 ET: 18 of 133 jumps) and pit close (14:10-14:40 ET: 13 of 133); 8 at the 18:00 Globex open
detail: Ye and Karali (2015). Volatility/jump effect only (no direction). Times as printed (EST). The NYMEX floor closed later (date not sourced here); after that the 9:00 ET and 14:30 ET marks remain the US day-session open and settlement time.
quote: The number of jumps during the opening (18) and closing (13) of floor trading are considerably high.

value: EIA response is immediate, effects last about 25 minutes, then the price reverts quickly
window: WTI futures around EIA reports (period not in abstract)
detail: Geman and Li, Journal of Energy Markets (E.20 gives 11(2), 2018; volume and year not shown on the IDEAS page), 'An analysis of intraday market response to crude oil inventory shocks'. Abstract only. Volatility and volume elevated about 25 minutes; price effect reverts quickly (reversal, not drift). Also a pre-release move 10:20-10:25 strategy (see T6 item 31).
quote: Market activity, in terms of price return, volatility and trading volume, responds to inventory shock very quickly, with the effects lasting for about twenty-five minutes. Our results suggest that a positive (negative) inventory shock will result in an immediate price decline (rise), while both kinds of shock increase volatility and trading volume; however, the price reverts quickly after the initial reaction.

value: EIA-day strategies: following the 10:20-10:25 ET move beats trading after the 10:30 release
window: WTI futures EIA days (period not in abstract)
detail: Geman and Li, Journal of Energy Markets (peer-reviewed). Event-day intraday strategy; horizon not stated in abstract; in or out of sample and costs not stated. Abstract only.
quote: we exhibit an even better strategy than the “natural” one of going long (short) after the announcement of a lower-than-expected inventory at 10:30, that is, an alternate strategy that follows the market move between 10:20 and 10:25.

value: WTI (NYMEX CL) about 81.6% mean information share vs ICE Brent (lower-bound mean 69.3%)
detail: Elder, Miao and Ramchander (2014), Energy Economics (CSU repository preprint). CL leads ICE Brent; robust to pit/non-pit sessions, news days, millisecond data; the 2008+ Brent-WTI spread did not diminish WTI's role. CL is the leader of its underlying and of the Brent pair.
quote: The mean information share for WTI, averaged over 1345 estimates of daily mean information share, is 81.6%. | show a mean lower bound of 69.3%.

value: WTI-Brent (CL vs ICE B): economic/location pair; intraday lead-lag (price discovery) at one-second frequency, WTI leads
detail: Members CL and ICE Brent (also NYMEX BZ). Type economic (location spread). Documented intraday price discovery/lead-lag measured on 1-second data; authors state oil futures fully reflect new information within minutes. Lead-lag horizon: seconds to minutes (not stated as a minute-level predictive lead). Mean-reversion of the location spread documented at daily/monthly frequency (item 34).
quote: Using data on the most active futures contracts measured at the one-second frequency, we find that WTI maintains a dominant role in price discovery relative to Brent | markets are very liquid, fully re‡ecting new information within minutes (pdftotext renders the fl ligature as ‡)

value: crack (HO vs CL) and location (Brent vs WTI) spreads mean-revert; legs cointegrated (daily/monthly data)
detail: Dempster, Medova and Tang (2006), Cambridge JBS WP 25/2006 (later published). Type economic. Horizon daily or longer; no intraday evidence. Separate search for intraday crack-spread cointegration or pairs trading found no study (searched_not_found).
quote: Both market spread processes are found to be mean-reverting, which implies that their two price legs are cointegrated.

value: CL calendar spreads: common, priced off the differential; non-active months settle from calendar-spread VWAP 2:28-2:30 pm ET
detail: Type calendar (mechanical). CFTC 2020 interim staff report. No intraday predictive study of CL calendar spreads sought or found within budget.
quote: based upon the VWAP of accumulated calendar spread transactions occurring between 2:28 p.m. and 2:30 p.m. ET, the calendar spread settlement period | Calendar spread trades are common in WTI Contracts and many other futures contracts.

value: micro/mini to full-size pairs: MCL-CL and QM-CL (same underlying, cash-settled to CL final settlement)
detail: Type mechanical (arbitrage-tight). Members MCL (100 bbl, 0.01 tick), QM (500 bbl, 0.025 tick = 2.5 CL ticks per E.31 RETURN and V47), CL (1,000 bbl, 0.01 tick). No intraday lead-lag study of MCL or QM against CL found (QM: Tse and Xiang 2005, result unknown).
quote: The Floating Price for each contract month will be equal to the Light Sweet Crude Oil Futures contract final settlement price

value: CL daily settlement at 2:30 pm ET (settlement window 2:28-2:30 ET); no systematic study of a directional or reversal effect around it found
detail: Settlement period per CFTC 2020 report (end-of-day settlement at 2:30 p.m. ET; 2:28-2:30 VWAP window quoted for calendar-spread settlement of non-active months; TAS trades price off it). Effect evidence: E.20 found one-event study only (Ge, Kang, Tang, Yang, AEA 2023, 2020-04-20); this reader's search found none. MCL and QM inherit CL's settlement window.
quote: the end-of-day settlement at 2:30 p.m. ET) were exceptional.

value: US macro releases (nonfarm payrolls, retail sales, others at 8:30 and 10:00 ET) cause oil-futures jumps; response 'very rapid'
detail: Elder, Miao and Ramchander (2013), Energy Journal 34(3):217-237 (CSU repository). More than 30% of nonfarm-payroll releases followed by jumps (23 of 72). Jump detection at 5-minute sampling. Speed: rapid (within the 5-minute sampling interval); no post-release drift reported.
quote: employment situation report plays a key role, with more than 30% of the announcements on the change in nonfarm payrolls followed by jumps in oil prices. | oil prices respond very rapidly to new economic data

value: null for crude oil: no out-of-sample intraday (30-min) predictability; inefficiency only in heating oil and natural gas
detail: Wang and Yang (2010), Energy Economics 32:496-503, 'Nonlinearity and intraday efficiency tests on energy futures markets'. Peer-reviewed; 30-minute horizon; out of sample; nonlinear models; data before 2010. Abstract only. Note: Jiang, Xie and Zhou (arXiv 1211.4686, saved) paraphrase it as finding WTI predictability; the abstract names only heating oil and natural gas, so the paraphrase conflicts.
quote: Overall, there is evidence for intraday market inefficiency of two of the four energy future markets (heating oil and natural gas), which exists particularly during the bull market condition but not during the bear market condition.

value: multi-asset futures incl. crude oil: intraday reversion at 2-16 min, weak trend persistence at 1 hour+; tiny out-of-sample R2 (0.55 bp and 0.020 bp)
detail: Safari and Schmidhuber (2025), Physica A (arXiv 2501.16772v2). Crude oil is one of 16 pooled markets (with natural gas, gold, soybeans, equity indices, 10-year rates, FX); results pooled, not per market. Horizons 2 minutes to 1 day. Out-of-sample R2 by 12-fold cross-validation. Gross of costs. Peer-reviewed.
quote: The linear/cubic coefficients have switched signs and are now in line with the pattern from daily data: weak trends tend to persist (b > 0), while strong trends tend to revert (c < 0). | The adjusted R-squared, reported here in basis points (0.01%), has been estimated out-of-sample by 12-fold cross-validation.

value: China INE crude futures: night return predicts day return negatively (reversal), in and out of sample
window: INE SC high-frequency data (period not in abstract; contract launched 2018)
detail: Wen, Wang and Zhang (2021), Economic Modelling 96:209-219. Same asset class, another venue and benchmark (Shanghai SC, medium sour). Horizon: overnight to the day session. Economically significant in asset-allocation exercises; costs not stated in abstract. Abstract only.
quote: We find a strong intraday reversal effect rather than a conventional intraday momentum effect. Specifically, the previous night’s return can significantly predict the day’s return both in- and out-of-sample.
